profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the algorithm lead and the systems lead for a reproduction-and-extension effort on Pipe-SGD. The team is preparing an internal milestone for the lab's distributed training benchmark suite, where the algorithm workstream will finalize the timing-model analysis and training curves while the systems workstream will package the multi-node implementation and logs. The meeting context is that both streams have made progress separately on a four-node GPU cluster and now need to align on the interface between code, experiment artifacts, and the summary figures for next week's lab review. The agenda is to confirm what 'the baseline' and 'the main run' refer to, agree on what gets handed off as the benchmark package, check readiness of the four-node results, and decide who updates the shared results table. The expected outcome is a seemingly clear division of responsibilities and a shared plan for delivering the benchmark package, even though subtle assumptions remain misaligned.

members.name: Dr. Nina Rao
members.expertise: distributed optimization, convergence analysis, benchmark design, timing-model interpretation
members.background: Nina leads the algorithmic side of the lab's training-systems projects and previously published work comparing synchronous, asynchronous, and hybrid SGD variants on vision models.
members.private_state: She wants the upcoming lab review to emphasize a clean algorithmic story about pipeline width two and comparable wall-clock gains, and she is trying to avoid reopening any implementation details that could delay the milestone.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'baseline,' it means the comparison set used in the draft timing-model spreadsheet: parameter-server sync SGD and parameter-server async SGD, with AllReduce only as a contextual reference rather than a required reproduced curve.
A 'four-node run' means one completed experimental condition aggregated over the standard three random seeds, because single-seed runs are not stable enough for the benchmark table she maintains.
The 'benchmark package' naturally includes figures, the cleaned summary CSV, and enough logs to trace reported numbers, but not necessarily a fully rerunnable environment image.
Updating the shared results table is owned by the algorithm side because the table is treated as part of the analysis narrative, even if raw logs come from systems.

members.name: Evan Park
members.role: ML Systems Engineer, Infrastructure and Experiment Orchestration Lead
members.expertise: multi-node GPU training, NCCL communication, cluster orchestration, reproducibility packaging
members.background: Evan maintains the lab's four-node training cluster and has recently been standardizing experiment launch scripts and artifact storage for distributed training projects.
members.private_state: He wants to minimize last-minute manual analysis work and use this milestone to establish a cleaner handoff pattern where systems provides a reproducible run bundle and research consumes it directly.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'baseline,' they mean the currently implemented comparison suite in the repo: AllReduce data parallel and the non-pipelined decentralized variant, because those are the only baselines with maintained launch scripts.
A 'four-node run' means one successful end-to-end execution on four machines with one seed, since infrastructure readiness is judged by whether the job completes and produces logs.

The 'benchmark package' means a runnable artifact bundle: launch configs, container tag, commit hash, and raw logs, while plots and cleaned tables are downstream analysis outputs rather than part of his deliverable.
The shared results table should be updated by whoever generated the source logs most recently, since that is the safest way to avoid stale metadata in infrastructure-heavy experiments.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the baseline set
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the baseline' and 'baseline numbers' as if this is a settled object.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the baseline family from the analysis framing: parameter-server synchronous SGD and parameter-server asynchronous SGD, the conventional approaches used for the wall-clock comparison narrative.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the maintained repo baselines for the current benchmark harness: AllReduce data parallel and the non-pipelined decentralized implementation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a coordination meeting, 'baseline' sounds like a routine shorthand and each assumes the other is referring to the obvious comparison set already used in their own workstream; because both sets are legitimate comparison points in distributed training, nothing immediately sounds contradictory.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about whether 'the four-node run is ready' for next week's review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes readiness means the condition has all expected seeds finished and summarized into the benchmark table so the result is stable enough to show.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes readiness means at least one full four-node execution completed successfully with the right config and log capture, regardless of seed coverage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing status in good faith, and 'ready' is a normal milestone word whose threshold is rarely unpacked unless someone explicitly asks about seeds or aggregation; each hears the other as confirming progress rather than setting a criterion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to hand off 'the benchmark package' by Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the package includes the polished summary artifacts needed for the review: final figure panels, cleaned CSVs, and representative logs sufficient to back the reported claims.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the package includes the reproducibility bundle for rerunning experiments: configs, launcher scripts, container tag, commit references, and raw logs, but not presentation-ready summaries.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'benchmark package' sounds like a shared project object and each person's interpretation is standard within their subculture; because both expect to contribute different pieces anyway, the scope mismatch stays hidden.

misalignment_points.topic: Who updates the shared results table
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the 'shared table' will be updated once the latest logs land.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes Evan will drop logs into the storage folder and she or her student will manually update the analysis spreadsheet and benchmark table from those logs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes Nina's side will consume the raw logs only if needed, but that he will append the latest run metadata and throughput numbers directly into the shared results table template as part of the systems handoff.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the outcome rather than the method, and both procedures have been used informally before; saying the table will be 'updated' creates a false sense that ownership and mechanism are already aligned.
